extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and students/practitioners interested in international relations and private international law
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science style essay describing the nature, sources, and practical problems of private international law and the development of international postal/telegraphic conventions in the 19th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of private international law
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules which serve to solve conflicts can and should be the same the world over, notwithstanding the diversity of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private international law seeks unity not by imposing uniform legislation (impractical among sovereign nations) but by establishing common rules—via concurrence of consent, treaties, or customs—to resolve conflicts of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private international law cannot be formed by unilateral legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: It can not be formed, like the civil law of each people, by legislation, or command of a superior authority, since independent sovereign nations recognize no authority superior to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no superior legislative authority exists over sovereign states, private international law must rest on agreements (express or implied) among states rather than on a single state's statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources: treaties and international customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Private international law, considered as a positive law, reposes on the agreements expressed or implied, which are entered into between sovereign nations. The law of nations is principally a customary law, which is founded on the tacit consent of the peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties are explicit agreements between states; international customs (tacit consent) function as implied treaties and are the principal source of private international law when treaties are few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between international customs and national customs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a vast difference between the international customs and the customs which form one of the sources of the civil law of each state: the latter have the force of law (tacit laws), while the international customary right are, strictly speaking, implied treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because international customs are founded on concurrence between sovereigns they occupy the place of agreements rather than of laws; the conditions for their formation therefore differ from those for national customary law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of tacit treaties requires concurrence of wills
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain rules common to all nations can not be formed but by a concurrence of consent, express or implied. The treaties are formed by a concourse of wills, and the laws are promulgated by way of commandment; the conditions under which tacit treaties can be formed should differ from the conditions under which implied laws are formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International customary rules (tacit treaties) presuppose general implied consent of nations and cannot be imposed by unilateral state action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of foreigner and citizen as a foundational principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The equality of the foreigner and the citizen is the basis of the private international law: if the foreigner did not enjoy any civil rights, it would not be a question by what law his rights were to be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private international law presumes foreigners are owed the same civil (private) rights everywhere as a matter of human rights (distinct from political rights), and this presumption underpins the need for rules to determine applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and universality of private rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil or private rights are certain faculties, the exercise of which is necessary to man for his physical, intellectual, and moral existence. These rights appertain to him simply as a man—they belong to him everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private rights are conceived as universal human faculties that should be exercisable irrespective of national frontiers; this philosophical stance supports harmonizing rules in private international law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-of-law problems to be resolved by private international law
rubrics_metrics.description: When laws of different nations conflict the judge must decide: is it the national law which the judge should apply, or that of the parties to the suit? Shall we take into account the law of the place where the subject of the dispute is situated? Shall we distinguish whether they are chattels or immovables? If arising upon contract, shall we have recourse to the law of the place where the contract is made, or where it is to be executed? Shall we give a preference to the law of the debtor or to that of the creditor? If instruments in writing are involved, shall we follow the law of the place where the writings were made?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private international law must develop principles to guide judges on choice-of-law questions across categories (contracts, property, instruments) and between competing connecting factors (lex loci, nationality, debtor/creditor interests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties as the only diplomatic means to reconcile sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one means of conciliating nations who recognize no superior authority, and that is by way of concurrence of consent. Treaties alone can put an end to the war of conflicting interests and diverse laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sovereign states accept no external authority, formal treaties (express agreements) are the primary diplomatic instrument to achieve uniformity or coordination in private international matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal treaty essentials (practical provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two countries who wish to regulate their international postal exchanges in a secure way must come to an understanding on the means of transportation they will use, what contribution to the expense of carriage will be made by the respective parties, what will be the expense of mails, whether the postage will be paid by the sender or receiver, and in what proportion the expenses will be borne by the offices cooperating in this transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal treaties must cover transportation modalities (rail, stage, steamers, sailing), cost-sharing and remuneration, who pays postage, transit arrangements including intermediaries, and distinctions between maritime and terrestrial transits (subsidies, gratuitous transport by railroads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal convention subjects: scope of items carried and transit regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties must regulate the transit, the manner in which it is to be effected, and the remuneration. They must also regulate what will be carried by the mails—letters, journals, pamphlets, packages of merchandise, money and valuables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As international postal exchanges expanded, conventions needed to define permitted classes of mail, handling rules, liability, and compensation for transit through intermediate countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between treaty and administrative regulation in postal unions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between the treaty and the detailed regulation for the execution of the treaty: the first can not be modified or amended but by the action of representatives fortified with the full powers of their Governments (a diplomatic act), while the other can be agreed upon between the administrators of the various postal departments (an administrative arrangement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International postal cooperation employs both binding diplomatic treaties for principles and more flexible administrative regulations for operational details, allowing managers to adapt procedures without renegotiating treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: International conferences and unions as mechanisms for harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: International conferences (e.g., Paris 1863, Berne 1874) were convened to consider and proclaim general principles 'of a nature to facilitate the relations of people with each other by way of the post, and to serve as a basis to international conventions.' These conferences laid the foundation for unions such as the General Postal Union and Telegraphic Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular international meetings of postal/telegraphic administrators and government delegates help identify general principles, encourage negotiation of treaties, and evolve both diplomatic and administrative instruments toward uniformity (lower rates, simplification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical obstacles to international uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties to forming international conventions include geographic separation, enormous inequality of territories, diversity of economic and financial views, existing arrangements, and the financial consequences for some states of joining new systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that political, economic, and administrative disparities complicate treaty-making; effective harmonization requires addressing financial burdens, entrenched bilateral arrangements, and divergent national interests.
